projects.title: Hierarchical Latent Variable Models for Neural Data Analysis · UC San Diego Capstone (HDSI)
projects.description: Mentored by Prof. Mikio AoiNeural recording methods are advancing faster in volume and speed than the methods used to analyze them. Using the International Brain Laboratory dataset (neural activity recorded from mice during a visual decision-making task), we applied variational latent Gaussian processes (vLGP) for dimensionality reduction and probabilistic canonical correlation analysis (pCCA) to relate activity across brain regions in a shared latent space. Using RMSE, we found that three latent variables captured the signal well, with diminishing returns beyond that.

Learned a lot at the Agent Hack Day w/ Wordware (YC S24) , Blaxel (YC X25) , and HackerSquad this weekend. One of the coolest things about these hacks is it’s a testing ground for our latest product features. We see what hackers can actually build with them, what works, and what we can improve upon. One example: the best use of Redis winning project Reloop, a self-improving agent that can remember past failures and uses that info to improve retries. It stores each failure in Redis, indexes them with RediSearch, and pulls back relevant ones before the next attempt. They also used Redis Context Retriever, which allowed them to not just store memory, but make it usable by the agent at the right moment. Very well executed 👏 Congrats again to Nihal Nihalani , Yahya Alhinai & Charlie Gillet on the win! We had some cracked sponsors, organizers and technical leaders this time around, special thanks to Simba Khadder , Guillaume Roux-Romestaing , Adam Chan , Sri Kalimani , Amy Zheng , Hermine (Hemi) de Menthiere , Mathis Joffre , and Paul Sinaï for making this event a reality. When production goes down, the hardest part isn't fixing it, it's figuring out what changed. That 30-60 minute scramble through dashboards and logs is still the norm at most companies. Last week at the Deep Agents Hackathon in SF, my team built Pager0, an incident response agent that reduces that scramble to ~47 seconds by calling the engineer's phone directly. No dashboards or laptop needed! 📞 We placed: 1st 🥇 Most Innovative Project Using Macroscope 3rd 🥉 Best Use of Auth0 for AI Agents Instead of stopping at a chat summary, Pager0 runs an end-to-end pipeline: 1. Detect the incident 2. Diagnose it with LLM-powered analysis 3. Identify the specific code changes causing the incident using Macroscope + GitHub 4. Call the on-call engineer's phone and let them approve fixes directly via Auth0 CIBA 5. Generate structured reports for engineers and executives #AIAgents #DevOps #IncidentResponse #Auth0 #Hackathon ...more

Over the weekend, my team won the $10,000 Patronus AI sponsor prize at the OpenEnv Hackathon in San Francisco. The challenge we tackled: how do you train LLM agents to resist prompt injection and manipulation in real enterprise workflows? We built SentinelOps Arena, a multi-agent reinforcement learning environment designed to train LLM agents to resist manipulation in enterprise systems. The core idea is that three AI agents compete in a simulated company environment: • Attacker (Red Team) launches attacks like schema drift, policy drift, social engineering, and rate limiting • Worker (Blue Team) must complete enterprise tasks (CRM, billing, ticketing) while resisting manipulation • Oversight Agent (Auditor) monitors behavior, flags violations, and explains failures All three agents are trained simultaneously through Group Relative Policy Optimization, each improving alongside the others. Huge thanks to the organizers at Cerebral Valley and the judges and mentors from Meta , Hugging Face , and many other organizations for making this event possible. 3rd place at IBM’s Austin Bobathon! 🥉 Two days into our internship, I got together with 5 other interns and spent a day building something completely from scratch and somehow, we ended up taking 3rd place out of 158 teams. We decided to tackle a problem that came up pretty quickly during our internship: AI is only as useful as the context you give it. At a company as large as IBM, there’s an incredible amount of knowledge being created every day. The problem is that a lot of it never makes it beyond the person or team that created it. Someone may have already solved the exact issue you're dealing with, but that solution could be sitting in an old chat, a local file, or buried in a previous AI conversation. Our idea was to give IBM Bob a way to actually remember that knowledge. We called it Bob Brain. We built a shared knowledge vault that Bob can interact with through an MCP server. Teams can save their notes, decisions, solutions, and context, and Bob can search through that information when it becomes relevant. What we made: • A FastAPI server for managing the knowledge vault • An MCP server with 8 tools for reading, searching, and writing • A VS Code/Bob extension for automatically syncing notes • A live knowledge graph connecting everything together One of our biggest challenges actually came from being three days into our internships. We didn't have access to much of IBM's internal cloud infrastructure yet, so we couldn't take the same approach as teams with access to hosted services. Instead, we built our own LAN-based syncing system to keep the vault in sync across our laptops. Huge thanks to the IBM Austin team for putting this together, and to my team Michael Tiburcio , Arya M. , Eric Wang , Jeffrey Xu , and Jaden C. for pulling this off in a day. #IBM #Bobathon

Over the past several months, I had the opportunity to develop a season brand campaign for the Orlando Magic as my senior capstone project at Florida Gulf Coast University. The campaign, Feel The Magic ( #FeelTheMagic ), was built around the idea of capturing the energy, excitement, and emotion that make live NBA basketball unforgettable. Rather than creating a single piece, I approached it like an actual team campaign. The project included: - A cinematic pregame jumbotron hype video designed to play before player introductions - A concept social media campaign - In-arena mockups, including the jumbotron, banners, billboards, and merchandise - Three promotional posters featuring Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner, and Desmond Bane This project challenged me to think beyond individual edits and consider how every piece of creative works together to build a cohesive brand identity across multiple platforms. As a lifelong Magic fan, this was an especially rewarding project to create, and it gave me the opportunity to combine my passion for basketball, storytelling, motion design, and branding into one campaign. I'd love to hear what you think! #NBA #OrlandoMagic #SportsMarketing #CreativeDirection #MotionDesign #VideoEditing #GraphicDesign #Branding #DigitalMedia #SportsCreative

Please like, comment and repost so we can win social media award for RocketRide Most promises don't get broken on purpose. Life just moves on. Today, four of us built a personal brain that catches them. It's called Nous. You type "I wanna meet with Kevin next week for dinner" and it works out who Kevin is, what you meant, and when it should happen. It connects to your calendar, email, messages, and event streams, so it knows what your week actually looks like and proposes a slot you've got nothing on. One tap books it. Show Nous how you handle something boring, like an invoice, once, and it learns how to handle the next one. But it refuses to act until you approve, which honestly took the most work. The whole thing runs on RocketRide. Every skill Nous learns compiles into a RocketRide pipeline, so the brain never executes anything itself, the engine does. We built a custom RocketRide node and turned their engine into the compilation target for a brain. Take RocketRide away and Nous can remember, but it can't act. FalkorDB is the living memory graph, Guild.ai agents review every skill before it can run, and LaserData streams events in as they happen. It's a second brain that keeps the promises your first one makes. Built at Memory Meets Motion. Thanks to Devnovatee and frontiertower for hosting. "Getting into a research lab is way easier than most people think." I learned that from P.J. Utz, the founder and faculty director of Stanford SIMR. The wildest thing he ever told me had nothing to do with the actual research. ... It was that most people never get into a lab for one reason: they never send the email. I didn't believe him at first. I thought if you weren't a nepo baby with four Nature journal publications or 4x legacy, you were cooked. Turns out none of that is true. Here's what actually is: - Most professors AREN'T gatekeepers waiting to reject you. A lot of them are quietly short on hands. If they genuinely need help, you reaching out isn't a bother, it's useful to them. I've had professors follow up with me. - The worst case isn't humiliation. It's silence. If they don't need anyone right now, they just won't reply. That's the entire risk everyone's so afraid of. - You also don't need to write three paragraphs about how their 2019 paper changed your life. They can tell when it's forced. Just say what you can actually do and leave it there. And if you've already done summer research training, safety, axess protocols, all of it, you're more prepared than you feel. A short resume and two honest sentences is enough. Before this post I camped the Stanford CIRM building and this is what one of the PhD lab interns I approached said: "If you're still in high school, it can genuinely be easier, not harder." I spent way too long waiting until I felt "ready" to reach out. That feeling never really shows up. You just send the email. If you're in a similar spot and want to talk through it, feel free to reach out. ~ aayu
